name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Friday 19 December 1975

clue.text: Six hours and the bills are due!

blocks.note: first meaning: a quarter of a twenty-four-hour day
second meaning: one of the four days in the year when rents and accounts fall due

explanation.surface: A householder groans that within six hours a pile of bills must be paid.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the quarter days (Lady Day, Midsummer, Michaelmas, Christmas) were the traditional dates for paying rent and settling accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: Six hours is literally one quarter of a day, and the traditional rent-paying dates are called quarter days.

blocks.note: surface reading: some woman who inspires stargazers
setter's reading: the Greek Muse who presides over astronomy

explanation.surface: A woman is the muse who spurs stargazers on.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth each Muse inspires one art, and the Muse of astronomy is named for the heavens.

blocks.note: first meaning: ribbons worn as tokens or badges, an old spelling of ribbons
second meaning: read as two words, bands round the ribs

explanation.surface: A shopper asks whether chest straps would make good party favours.
explanation.walkthrough: A favour here is a ribbon or rosette worn as a token; ribband is an archaic spelling of ribbon.
explanation.definitionFit: Ribbands are ribbons worn as badges or tokens, and split up they are bands round one's rib cage.

clue.text: Shield with one's arms to avoid blotting?

definitions.note: a cryptic hint: the thing one keeps free of blots

blocks.note: first meaning: the heraldic shield displaying a coat of arms
second meaning: what one must not put a blot on, in the idiom about disgrace

explanation.surface: Someone raises their arms like a shield to keep off ink blots.
explanation.walkthrough: A blot on one's escutcheon is a stain on one's reputation, so this is the thing you avoid blotting.
explanation.definitionFit: An escutcheon is the shield bearing a family's heraldic arms, and the idiom 'blot on one's escutcheon' means a disgrace.

clue.text: Dippy procedure for a not very colourful monarch

blocks.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown
a king is a monarch

explanation.surface: A drab king is subjected to some daft ritual.
explanation.walkthrough: Dippy looks like it means silly, but here it means involving dipping.
explanation.definitionFit: Dunking is the act of dipping something, such as a biscuit into tea, so it is a procedure of dipping.

indicators.note: sound tells us to go by how the words are spoken, not written

blocks.note: to avail oneself of something is to use it

explanation.surface: Someone takes advantage of some healthy trees.
explanation.walkthrough: Sound looks like an adjective (healthy) describing the trees, but it is the signal that the word is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Yews are evergreen conifers often grown in churchyards, so they are trees.

blocks.note: surface reading: a devotee of some obscure deity
setter's reading: a citizen of the city whose altar was inscribed 'To an unknown god', as Paul notes in Acts 17

explanation.surface: A follower of some obscure god is described.
explanation.walkthrough: In Acts 17, Paul tells the people of Athens he found their altar inscribed 'To an unknown god'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible records the citizens of Athens keeping an altar to an unknown god, so they worshipped one.

clue.text: Is now the time to take someone to court?

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase, now an adverb

definitions.text: the time to take someone to court

blocks.note: first meaning: the current era

blocks.clueFragment: the time to take someone to court
blocks.note: second meaning: read as two words, the day a debutante is presented at the royal court

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether now is the moment to sue.
explanation.walkthrough: Court here is the royal court, where young women were once formally presented, not a court of law.
explanation.definitionFit: The present day means the current time, and read literally it is the day for presenting someone at court.

blocks.note: first meaning: further to the east, comparative of east
second meaning: the Christian spring feast of the Resurrection

explanation.surface: A festival is said to be more eastern in flavour than others.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter can be read as the comparative of east, and it is also the principal Christian spring feast.

clue.text: Horse I'm able to find in London

definitions.note: the definition describes a place to be found in London

blocks.note: a barb is a breed of North African horse
I'm able is I can

explanation.surface: Someone boasts they can track down a horse in London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Barbican is an arts centre and housing estate in the City of London, named after the old fortified outwork on the site.
explanation.definitionFit: The Barbican is a well-known district and arts complex in the City of London, so it is something you find there.

clue.text: They appear to make no progress in airborne search

definitions.text: They appear to make no progress in airborne search

blocks.clueFragment: They appear to make no progress
blocks.note: surface reading: people or vehicles stuck and going nowhere
setter's reading: birds of prey that hang motionless in the air while hunting

explanation.surface: An air search team seems to be getting nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a failing rescue flight; the answer is a bird famous for hovering in one spot while scanning for prey.
explanation.definitionFit: Kestrels hunt by hovering on the wind, staying still in the sky while watching the ground for voles.

indicators.note: in says one item sits within the others, so the article is placed among the directions

blocks.note: south, west and north as compass letters
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper article is cut in three different ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawn is the past participle of saw, meaning cut through with a toothed blade.

clue.text: For the time being an indicator is used

definitions.note: a cryptic description of a clock pointer, a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: the clock pointer marking the passing seconds
second meaning: previously owned

explanation.surface: A makeshift pointer is pressed into service for the time being.
explanation.walkthrough: For the time being reads as a stock phrase meaning temporarily, but it describes a pointer indicating the time.
explanation.definitionFit: The second hand is the clock pointer that sweeps the seconds, and second-hand goods are already used.

blocks.note: first meaning: the answer to 18-down, a family member
second meaning: a transfer from one train to another

explanation.surface: A relative travels to a railway station for a change of scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A connection is a family member by blood or marriage, and also a transfer between trains at a station.

clue.text: What a cross fairy intended to try? I hear

indicators.note: I hear says the phrase must be listened to, judged by how it is spoken

blocks.note: a cross is the letter X, written out as it is said
a peri is a fairy of Persian legend
intended means meant

explanation.surface: An angry fairy's wicked plan is described, as overheard.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken aloud, ex-peri-meant is what a cross fairy meant. A peri is a fairy in Persian myth, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To experiment is to test something out, which is to try it as a verb.

blocks.note: Charles, a name of Swedish kings, shortened to its abbreviation Chas
the numeral of King Charles X of Sweden, X being ten

explanation.surface: A Swedish monarch, cut down to size, imposes discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles X of Sweden is written as Chas (the short form of Charles) followed by ten, the Roman X.
explanation.definitionFit: To chasten is to discipline or correct someone, especially by punishment, so the verbs match.

blocks.note: first meaning: moves forward
second meaning: approaches made to someone, often romantic

explanation.surface: A concert proceeds with its opening orchestral pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: Overtures suggests orchestral openings, but here it means approaches made to a person.
explanation.definitionFit: To advance is to move forward, and advances are approaches or propositions made to someone.

blocks.note: to spur is to goad or urge on
Ned is a pet form of Edward

explanation.surface: Someone scorned the idea of needling a man called Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: To spurn is to reject with contempt, so spurned matches disdained as a past-tense verb.

blocks.note: first meaning: bearing on the matter in hand
second meaning: the answer to 13-across, a family member

explanation.definitionFit: Relative can mean relevant or pertinent, as in relative to the question, and also a family connection.

clue.text: Exercise supervision in place of bishop

definitions.note: a cryptic hint: what a bishop does over his see

blocks.note: first meaning: to supervise
second meaning: read as two words, being above the bishop's diocese, his see

explanation.surface: Someone takes charge while standing in for the bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is a bishop's diocese; to be over the see is to supervise it.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee is to supervise work or people, and split up it is to be in charge over a bishop's see.

clue.text: Some of Lear's repeat line to be on hire purchase

definitions.note: the answer is the noun in the phrase on the never-never

blocks.note: first meaning: part of King Lear's line of five repeated nevers over the dead Cordelia
second meaning: British slang for buying on instalments

explanation.surface: Part of a famous line from Lear is said to be bought on credit.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's line in Shakespeare is 'Never, never, never, never, never!'. In Britain, buying on the never-never means hire purchase, paying in instalments.
explanation.definitionFit: Hire purchase is jokingly called the never-never because the payments seem never to end.

blocks.note: first meaning: a brightly coloured Australasian parrot
second meaning: the character who swims in Alice's pool of tears in Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: A pet parrot is pictured paddling in a flood of weeping.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, a Lory is among the creatures in the Pool of Tears.
explanation.definitionFit: A lory is a small brightly plumaged parrot of Australasia, and Carroll's Lory swims in the pool of tears.

definitions.note: a cryptic hint at a cannabis cigarette

blocks.note: first meaning: a short thick double-breasted coat
second meaning: a joint, made from the hemp plant cannabis

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a jacket is made of hemp cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: Hemp is cannabis, and reefer is slang for a cannabis cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A reefer is a heavy sailor's jacket, and also slang for a marijuana cigarette, which is made of hemp.

blocks.note: to hang someone is to execute them
over means finished, after it is done

explanation.surface: Bad blood lingers after a hanging.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces run in reverse clue order: the execution comes first, then over for after. Ill-feeling here is bodily sickness, not resentment.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangover is the queasy, headachy sickness felt the morning after heavy drinking, a literal ill feeling.

blocks.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
east and south, two compass points

explanation.surface: Players compete for six points in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: To vie is to contend or strive against others, so vies matches competes.

blocks.note: she in the plural, women
a Riff is a Berber of the Rif mountains of Morocco

explanation.surface: Berber women act as keepers of the peace.
explanation.walkthrough: The Riffs (or Rifs) are Berbers of northern Morocco. There is no container signal: the Berber is simply set among the women, read as she in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheriffs are law officers charged with keeping public order, so they are keepers of the peace.

clue.text: Sewer would be unnecessary head with ship attached aft

indicators.note: attached aft says the answer is the longer word once the trailing addition is taken back off its end

blocks.note: needless means unnecessary
surface padding, most likely a garbled 'had' in the newspaper text
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A drain would be pointless if a ship were fixed to its stern.
explanation.walkthrough: Sewer means one who sews, not a drain. Add SS to the answer and it becomes needless. The newspaper text around 'head' is garbled, probably 'had' in print.
explanation.definitionFit: A needle is the tool that does the sewing, so it is literally a sewer, one who sews.

blocks.note: first meaning: the centre of a sweet, read as two words
second meaning: a beloved person

explanation.surface: Someone asks their darling what filling a chocolate has.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetheart is a beloved partner, an endearment like darling, and split up it is a sweet's centre.
